docsis_monitor.json — everything docsis_monitor does.
Install at ~/config/docsis_monitor.json, or /etc/docsis_monitor.json
for a system service. Nothing here is a command-line flag: a monitor
is started once and left running for months, and a setting on a
command line is a setting nobody can find six months later.
One interface, by name. Not "any": a monitor that cannot say WHICH
wire went quiet cannot say anything worth acting on. This wants to
be the interface the CMTS relays reach the provisioning server on,
or a mirror of it.
Stay in the foreground. --nofork says the same for one run. It
detaches by default: a monitor that stops when somebody closes a
terminal is worse than no monitor, because the screen it was meant
to warn on stays quiet either way.
How many seconds of history a judgement is made over, and how often
the counts are written to ~/logs/docsis_monitor.log. Five minutes is
long enough that one slow minute is not an alarm and short enough
that a real outage is caught before the phone rings.

thresholds.//: Least fraction of those requests that must be answered, 0 to 1.
A server that is up, listening and failing everything looks
exactly like one that is down. Not evaluated until a handful have
arrived: a ratio over three packets is noise.
The longest silence that is normal on a CMTS interface nobody has
measured, in seconds. Deliberately generous: an interface nobody
has looked at should not be the one that wakes somebody up.
How long the same trap is not repeated for, in seconds. An outage
lasting an afternoon is one problem, not fifty. A CHANGE always
goes out -- quiet to unanswered, or recovery -- however recently

//: A plant is not one thing. One interface carries several thousand
modems and should never be silent for five minutes; another carries
forty and is properly silent for an hour. One number over the whole
plant is wrong for both: set for the busy one it cries wolf about
the quiet one every night, and set for the quiet one it says nothing
for an hour after the busy one falls over.
Keyed on the gi-address, which is what the relay stamps on a request
and what the server picks a pool from. Anything not named here uses
idle_seconds above.
Do not guess these. Run `docsis_monitor --adaptation 60`, which
watches for an hour and then writes a suggested block into the log,
measured from what the plant actually did.
SNMPv2c traps. No targets means the log only, which is a legitimate
way to run this: the counts are still written and still worth
reading. The community is a password sent in clear text, which is
what SNMPv2c is; it is here because receivers demand one.
Traps arrive under 1.3.6.1.4.1.99999: .1 quiet, .2 unanswered,
.3 recovered. Each carries the host, the interface, the state, the
requests, replies and TFTP reads counted, the window length, and the
busiest destination -- so an alert says where to look without
anybody logging in.

snmp.//: What the traps call this host. Defaults to its own name.

//: A trap goes to a network management platform, which not every plant
has. A mail relay, every plant has. The same finding, in a form
somebody reads on a phone at two in the morning: the subject carries
the host, the state and the counts, so nobody has to open it to find
out whether to get up.
Remove this section, or leave `to` empty, and no mail is sent.
PLAIN SMTP, no STARTTLS. This is for a relay on a network you trust,
which is the ordinary shape for alerting. `username` and `password`
are here because some relays insist on AUTH, and the password then
crosses the wire IN CLEAR TEXT. If the relay is not on a network you
trust, leave them out.
